title: The best point is a corner
objectives: Show that a linear programme’s optimum sits at a vertex, and find it on a picture.

screens.title: Slide the profit line
screens.prose: Every plan on the dashed line earns the same profit, $60x + 40y = c$ (£k). Slide $c$ up and the line moves away from the origin.

derive.caption: $60x + 40y$ = {{fixed(c, 0)}}: the line {{c <= 480.5 ? 'still touches the region' : 'has left the region'}}.

screens.question: Slide $c$ to the largest profit at which the line still touches the region.

hints.text: Watch the last point the line touches as it leaves.

feedback.correct: At $c = 480$ the line touches only the corner $(4, 6)$; it then passes through $(8, 0)$ and $(0, 12)$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Push the line out until one more step would leave the region empty under it.

byKey.past: The line has left the region: no plan earns that much.
byKey.early: Plans further out still touch the line; keep sliding.

explain.text: The line $60x + 40y = 480$ meets the region only at $(4, 6)$, so £480k is the best profit. The last point touched is a corner.

screens.title: A corner is two active limits
screens.prose: A **vertex** of the region is where two limits are active together. At the best corner the budget and the risk limit are both used up.
screens.question: Solve $x + y = 10$ and $3x + y = 18$. Give the vertex as $(x, y)$.

hints.text: Subtract the first equation from the second.

feedback.correct: $(4, 6)$. A linear objective on a bounded polygon is largest at a vertex, so we only need the corners.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the equations to remove $y$.

byKey.liq: $(5, 3)$ is where risk meets liquidity. Here the budget meets risk.

explain.text: $(3x + y) - (x + y) = 18 - 10$ gives $x = 4$, then $y = 6$. Two lines crossing, as in the equations course, is how every vertex is found.

screens.title: Every pair of limits
screens.prose: Five limits ($x + y \le 10$, $3x + y \le 18$, $x \le 5$, $x \ge 0$, $y \ge 0$) give 10 pairs. Each pair that crosses gives a candidate point; some break another limit.
screens.question: Complete the table: feasible or not, and the profit of the feasible points.

feedback.correct: Five pairs give the pentagon's corners, with profits 480, 400, 420, 300 and 0. $(5, 5)$, $(10, 0)$, $(0, 18)$ and $(6, 0)$ break a limit.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test each point against all five limits.

explain.text: Of the 10 pairs, one is parallel and four cross outside the region. The best of the five corners is $(4, 6)$, so enumerating vertices solves any small LP.

screens.title: A steeper profit line
screens.prose: Suppose A's profit rises from £60k to £150k per £m, B's staying at £40k. The profit line turns steeper than the risk edge, which has slope $-3$.
screens.question: Tap the new optimal vertex.

feedback.correct: $(5, 3)$, £870k. Once A earns more than $3 \times 40 = 120$ per £m, the line is steeper than the risk edge. The optimum jumps.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Price each corner with the new profits.

explain.text: At £150k, $(5, 3)$ earns 870, $(4, 6)$ 840 and $(5, 0)$ 750. The optimum moves from vertex to vertex as the objective turns past an edge's slope.

screens.title: A tie along an edge
screens.prose: Now both strategies earn £60k per £m. The profit line $60x + 60y = c$ is parallel to the budget edge.
screens.question: What profit does every plan on the edge from $(0, 10)$ to $(4, 6)$ earn, in £k?

feedback.correct: £600k along the whole edge. The optimum is not unique, but the vertices $(0, 10)$ and $(4, 6)$ are among the optimal points.

byKey.one: That is the rate per £m. The edge invests £10m.

explain.text: $60x + 60y = 60(x + y) = 600$ on the budget edge, and less elsewhere. With a tie, a whole edge is optimal, and a vertex is still among the best points.

screens.title: The simplex walk
screens.prose: The **simplex method** walks from vertex to vertex along edges, each step raising the profit. It stops when no edge improves.
screens.question: Put the walk in order. Leave out the steps that do not belong.

lines.text: Raise $x$: the limits allow 10, 6 and 5, so liquidity stops it at $(5, 0)$, £300k.
Raise $y$ along $x = 5$: risk stops it at $(5, 3)$, £420k.
Slide along the risk edge to $(4, 6)$, gaining £60k for each £1m moved out of A: £480k.
Stop: towards $(0, 10)$ loses £20k a unit, and back towards $(5, 3)$ loses £60k.
Jump to $(0, 10)$, because it invests the most money.
lines.why: $(0, 10)$ earns £400k. The walk follows edges that raise profit, not the amount invested.

lines.text: Stop at $(5, 0)$: it is a vertex, so it is optimal.
lines.why: Every vertex is a candidate, not the answer. An edge from $(5, 0)$ still improves.

hints.text: The ratio test: how far can $x$ rise before each limit binds?
Budget at 10, risk at 6, liquidity at 5: the smallest wins.
Then up to $(5, 3)$, along to $(4, 6)$, and stop.

feedback.correct: Three steps: £300k, £420k, £480k. At $(4, 6)$ both edges lose, so the walk stops.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each step moves along an edge and must raise the profit.

byKey.d1: That jump is not along an edge, and $(0, 10)$ is worse than $(4, 6)$.
byKey.d2: At $(5, 0)$ raising $y$ still earns £40k a unit.
byKey.left-out: You left out a step of the walk.

explain.text: Moving one unit from $(5, 3)$ towards $(4, 6)$ changes profit by $-60 + 3 \times 40 = +60$. From $(4, 6)$ the edges give $-60 + 40 = -20$ and $-60$, so no edge improves.

screens.title: Setting the gradient to zero
screens.prose: A habit from calculus: to find the best plan, set the gradient of the objective to zero. Here the objective is $60x + 40y$.
screens.question: Where does $\nabla(60x + 40y) = \mathbf{0}$ hold?

options.text: Nowhere: the gradient is $(60, 40)$ at every point, so the optimum must be on the boundary.
At the origin, where the profit is 0.
options.why: The gradient is $(60, 40)$ there too. A zero profit is not a zero gradient.

options.text: At the centre of the region, which balances the limits.
options.why: Inside the region profit can always rise by moving along $(60, 40)$.

hints.text: It is never zero, so no interior point can be best.

feedback.correct: The gradient is never zero. From any interior point, a step along $(60, 40)$ raises profit, so the optimum sits on the boundary.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute the gradient first.

byKey.origin: At the origin the gradient is still $(60, 40)$, pointing into the region.
byKey.centre: No interior point is optimal for a linear objective.

explain.text: $\nabla(60x + 40y) = (60, 40)$, a constant. Calculus finds no stationary point, and moving along the gradient always helps until a limit stops it.

screens.title: Why a vertex wins
screens.prose: Level 1 showed that a bounded polygon is the set of convex combinations of its vertices $\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_K$. We use that to prove a vertex is optimal.
screens.question: Put the argument in order. Leave out the lines that do not belong.

lines.text: Write any feasible $\mathbf{x}$ as $\sum_k \theta_k\mathbf{v}_k$ with $\theta_k \ge 0$ and $\sum_k \theta_k = 1$.
A weighted average is at most its largest term: $\sum_k \theta_k\,\mathbf{c}^T\mathbf{v}_k \le \max_k \mathbf{c}^T\mathbf{v}_k$.
So some vertex earns at least as much as any feasible point.

lines.why: The gradient is $\mathbf{c}$, never zero unless $\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{0}$.

lines.text: The objective is convex, so its maximum is at its stationary point.
lines.why: Convex functions have minima at stationary points, and a linear one has none.

hints.text: Start by writing $\mathbf{x}$ in terms of the vertices.
An average never beats its best term.

feedback.correct: Combination, linearity, average at most the maximum, conclusion.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Begin with a convex combination of vertices.

byKey.d1: The gradient of a linear function is the constant $\mathbf{c}$.
byKey.d2: The argument uses linearity and averages, not stationary points.
byKey.left-out: You left out a step of the argument.

explain.text: A linear function of a convex combination is the same combination of its values. Weights that sum to 1 cannot lift an average above its largest term, so the best vertex is optimal.

screens.title: Three limits at one corner
screens.prose: Add a sixth limit, $2x + y \le 14$. It passes through $(4, 6)$: $8 + 6 = 14$.
screens.question: What changes?

options.text: Nothing: the line cuts nothing off, and three limits now meet at $(4, 6)$.
The optimum moves, because a new limit is active.
options.why: Being active at the optimum is not the same as cutting it off. The optimum stays at $(4, 6)$.

hints.text: Every corner passes, so the region does not change.

feedback.correct: The region and the optimum are unchanged. Three active limits at one vertex is called **degenerate**. The simplex method can then take a step of length 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check every corner against the new line.

byKey.move: The new limit is active at $(4, 6)$ but removes no plan.

explain.text: Every corner satisfies $2x + y \le 14$, so the limit is redundant and touches the region only at $(4, 6)$. A region with no vertex at all, such as a half-plane, can only have a whole line of optima.

screens.title: A smart order router
screens.prose: The cheapest split of 10,000 shares fills venue 2 (0.25p) and venue 1 (0.30p) to capacity. The remaining 3,000 go to venue 3 (0.40p).
screens.question: How many constraints are active at this split?

hints.text: Count the capacities that are full.
Venues 1 and 2 are full; venue 3 is not.
The total $a + b + c = 10{,}000$ is always active, so three.

feedback.correct: Three, which pins down one point in three dimensions: a vertex. A router fills venues cheapest first until the fees change.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the full venues, then the total.

byKey.two: You counted the full venues. The equality for the total is active too.

explain.text: Three variables need 3 active constraints to fix a vertex: two capacities and the total. So the cheapest-first split is a corner of the feasible set, as the theory says.

ideas: A linear objective on a bounded polygon is largest at a vertex. There as many limits are active as there are variables.
Small problems can be solved by listing every vertex. The simplex method walks along improving edges and stops when none improves.
The optimum jumps between vertices as the objective turns past an edge; a tie makes a whole edge optimal.

formula.name: Vertex optimality
formula.note: Any feasible point is a convex combination of the vertices.

summary.trap: Setting the gradient of a linear objective to zero finds nothing: $\nabla(\mathbf{c}^T\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{c}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Price every corner.

quiz.prose: In the first simplex step we raise $x$ from $(0, 0)$ with $y = 0$.
quiz.question: How far can $x$ rise before the first limit binds?

feedback.correct: Budget allows 10, risk 6, liquidity 5: the smallest is 5.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the smallest of the three limits on $x$.

byKey.risk: Risk allows 6, but liquidity stops $x$ at 5 first.
byKey.bud: The budget allows 10, but two limits bind earlier.

explain.text: With $y = 0$: $x \le 10$, $3x \le 18$ and $x \le 5$. The ratio test takes the smallest, 5.

quiz.prose: A student claims a linear objective can be best at an interior point of a bounded feasible region.
quiz.question: When can an interior point be optimal?

options.text: Only when $\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{0}$, so every point ties.

options.why: If $\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{0}$ every point, interior ones included, is optimal.
Size does not matter: a nonzero $\mathbf{c}$ always improves from an interior point.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. From an interior point, a small step along $\mathbf{c}$ stays feasible.

explain.text: If $\mathbf{c} \ne \mathbf{0}$, a small step along $\mathbf{c}$ from an interior point stays feasible and raises $\mathbf{c}^T\mathbf{x}$ by $\epsilon|\mathbf{c}|^2$. So only $\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{0}$ allows an interior optimum.
